Most people think the problem with disagreeing in a second language is vocabulary. It almost never is. The problem is that the sentence arrives with no cushion. A native speaker who disagrees with you rarely says you are wrong. They say I take your point, and their voice goes up, and then they say but the timeline does not work for us, and their voice comes down. The rise tells you they heard you. The fall tells you they are not moving. Take the rise away and the same sentence sounds rude. Take the fall away and it sounds like you are about to give in. The second thing is the modal verbs. That might not work. We would need to check. I am not sure that would scale. None of those sentences is weaker than saying no. They are just as firm. They simply leave the other person a door to walk through, and people who have a door walk through it much faster than people who are facing a wall.

I have been on the vendor side of this conversation maybe two hundred times, so let me tell you which pushback works on me and which does not. Pushback that says your timeline is too long does nothing. I hear it every week, and I have learned that it usually means the bank has not looked at its own approval process. Pushback that works comes with three things. First, a constraint I can see, like a compliance review that takes ninety days and cannot be shortened. Second, a number, because a number turns an opinion into a problem we both have to solve. And third, a counterproposal, because if you only reject my plan, I will simply send you the same plan again next month with a new cover page. The banks I remember are the ones that said: we cannot do twelve months, here is why, and here is what we could do in four. I almost always said yes to them, and I almost never said yes to anybody who only said no.

There is a rule in procurement that I wish somebody had taught me when I was twenty-five. Never give a concession without getting one back. If you move on the price, they move on the scope. If you accept their settlement model, they accept your timeline. The moment you give something away for free, you have taught the other side that pushing works, and they will push harder in the next meeting. The second rule is about the past. When a project goes wrong, the tempting sentence is you should have told us. It is accurate, and it will cost you the relationship. The sentence that keeps the relationship is this could have been caught earlier, and here is how we make sure it is caught next time. Same fact, same criticism, but nobody in the room has to defend themselves, so everybody can start fixing it. Hold your ground on the substance, and be generous with the grammar.
